segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Spy films can be divided into two groups. The first is made up of thrillers whose narratives are built around manhunts and chases. Examples of this type are the Bulldog Drummond films and the adventures of Alfred Hitchcock (1899-1980), Foreign Correspondent (1940) and Saboteur (1942).

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The second group consists of existential thrillers adapted from authors such as Eric Ambler and Graham Greene, like Journey into Fear (1942) and Ministry of Fear (1943). These feature ordinary protagonists rather than professional secret agents and are characterized by a style somewhere between noir and expressionism.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The spy film reached its peak during the Cold War, when the genre became a vehicle for the geopolitical and ideological conflict between the free, democratic West and the totalitarian communist bloc. The first films of this period, such as I Was a Communist for the FBI (1951), are crude products of McCarthyist paranoia.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: When the "Red Scare" faded, filmmakers were able to take a more critical look at the espionage game. North by Northwest (1959), by Alfred Hitchcock (1899-1980), addresses the moral ambiguity of the Cold War, and the thriller The Manchurian Candidate (1962), by John Frankenheimer (1930-2002), explores the anxieties stirred by brainwashing, a typical Cold War theme, with a plot that sinisterly anticipates the assassination of President Kennedy in 1963.

segments.original: The spy films of the 1960s respond to events such as the construction of the Berlin Wall (1961) and the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962). The thriller is represented above all by the James Bond films, based on novels by Ian Fleming, beginning with Dr. No (1962), followed by From Russia with Love (1963).

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The 007 films are fundamentally different from the books in that the filmmakers replaced Fleming's Soviet villains with a supranational crime syndicate, freeing the screen Bond from the ideological context of the Cold War. The James Bond films combine visual spectacle (exotic locations, action sequences) with scenarios of consumerism and sexual permissiveness.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Box-office hits, the formula and the series have remained in almost continuous production to this day. Goldfinger (1964) and Thunderball (1965) mark the peak of "Bondmania." Although the later films in the series are mere repetitions of the same formula, James Bond remains the archetype of the secret agent of action, a model for other series such as Mission: Impossible and the Jason Bourne films.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: A countercycle of "anti-Bond" films in the mid-1960s brought a more ambiguous and cynical perspective. Martin Ritt (1914-1990) directed The Spy Who Came In from the Cold (1965), a faithful adaptation of the work of John Le Carré which, with its shabby antihero and austere black-and-white photography of bleak wintry locations, is the antithesis of the 007 films.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Their atmosphere of suspicion and moral ambiguity is closer to the existential anguish of film noir than to the fantastical world of James Bond. Michael Caine (b. 1933) plays the suburban spy Harry Palmer in three films based on novels by Len Deighton: The Ipcress File (1965), Funeral in Berlin (1966) and Billion Dollar Brain (1967). With their informants and double agents, these films reflect the reality of espionage as revealed in cases such as the Cambridge spy ring, whose members included Guy Burgess, Donald Maclean and Kim Philby.
